evidence.claims: Checked: b matches simulation 30.4 vs 29.0 and 61.2 vs 61.6 (results.txt section 0, backed); b/a 2.23/2.03/2.01 (backed); f* 0.81/0.90/0.57 (backed); pipeline sds and RMSE ratios 2.5x and 12% (0.520/0.212=2.45, 0.238/0.212=1.12, backed); coverage figures (backed). Not backed / wrong: README:3 'real data is the scarcer input unless a simulated job costs under about a third of a real pair' and paper:13 'real data wins per unit cost when kappa is above roughly a third' - the break-even where per-unit-cost value is equal (and f*=0.5) is kappa=2a/b = 0.897 (rho=0.5) to 0.988 (rho=0.8), i.e. a job at about half a pair's cost, and the README version has the direction backwards (cheap simulation means real data gets MORE of the budget: f*=0.97 at kappa=0.001). Paper:19 'four of five cells' at m>=20000: there are six such cells (0.930, 0.934, 0.948, 0.972, 0.916, 0.926); the 0.972 over-coverage is not mentioned. README:3 'restores 0.92-0.95 for m >= 1000' holds only for the n=200 row (n=1000, m=1000 is 0.888; n=1000, m=50000 is 0.972). Paper:19 / README:15 'even the twin's own interval under-covers (0.79-0.85)' cites coverage of the real W; no experiment measures coverage of the twin's own wait. README:9 says 6 tests; there are 8. Limits and 'stylised, no lab data' disclaimers are present and honest.
evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: the allocation of effort between collecting more input data and running more simulation is studied by Freimer & Schruben (2002, WSC, 'Collecting data and estimating parameters for input distributions'), Ng & Chick (2001 WSC; 2006 ACM TOMACS 'Reducing parameter uncertainty for stochastic systems'), and the input-uncertainty variance decomposition by Cheng & Holland (1997) and Song & Nelson (2015); simulation-only CIs under-covering under input error is the standard motivating example of Barton (2012) and Henderson (2003). The project cites Cheng & Holland, Barton, Whitt and Ankenman-Nelson but not the data-collection allocation papers, and presents the split as 'the trade-off left open'. The result is a correct closed-form M/M/1 instance of a Neyman-type allocation (minimise a/n + b/m under a linear budget) - a sound teaching example and a useful worked case, not a new result at the PhD/publishable bar research/CLAUDE.md sets. One model, exponential inputs, one pipeline configuration; no bootstrap or Bayesian input-uncertainty baseline is compared for the aware interval.
evidence.domain: Method matches standard practice: delta-method input variance with exponential MLEs (verified 13.0 / 61.0), the Daley 1968 / Whitt 1989 asymptotic variance of the M/M/1 customer-average delay (verified by simulation), stationary-start replications, Lagrange allocation (verified by grid), normal-theory coverage. A simulation methodologist would sign off on the mechanics with the stated limits; they would ask for a bootstrap/Bayesian-model-averaging interval as the comparator rather than only the delta method, and would note the ratio RMSE conditions on stable fits (E[W_hat] is infinite unconditionally).

defects.what: The qualitative decision rule is wrong: README says real data is the scarcer input 'unless a simulated job costs under about a third of a real pair' (direction reversed: cheaper simulation pushes MORE budget to real data, f*=0.97 at kappa=0.001) and the paper puts the per-unit-cost break-even at kappa about a third; it is kappa = 2a/b = 0.90 (rho=0.5) to 0.99 (rho=0.8), a job at about half a pair's cost, where f*=0.5.

Core outputs untested: 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive, including aware_ci dropping the input variance (the paper's recommended interval), optimal_split returning 1-f, the stationary start removed, and a wrong naive-coverage formula.

Nearest prior work on allocating effort between input-data collection and simulation runs (Freimer & Schruben 2002; Ng & Chick 2001, 2006; Song & Nelson 2015) is not cited; the split is presented as an open trade-off while the result is a closed-form M/M/1 instance of a standard Neyman-type allocation. Below the research/CLAUDE.md publishable bar on novelty; no bootstrap/Bayesian input-uncertainty interval as a baseline for the aware CI.
'Aware coverage at m >= 20 000 is 0.916-0.934 in four of five cells': there are six such cells; the other two are 0.948 and 0.972 (over-coverage, unmentioned).
'Even the twin's own interval under-covers (0.79-0.85)' cites coverage of the real W; no experiment measures the twin interval's coverage of the twin's own wait.
'restores 0.92-0.95 for m >= 1000' holds only for the n=200 row; n=1000, m=1000 gives 0.888 and n=1000, m=50000 gives 0.972.
README says '6 tests, ~2 s' and experiments '~1.5 min'; the suite has 8 tests (0.7 s) and the run takes about 58 s.

verdict: budget-twin's numbers are right: the headline run reproduces byte-for-byte, and independent numpy recomputations match a(rho) (13.06 vs 13.0), b(rho) (29.3 vs 29.0), every optimal split and penalty ratio, and the coverage formula, with an independent coverage re-run within 2-3 SE. It misses the bar on verification and claims: 4 of 5 seeded bugs in core logic survive the 8 tests (the input-aware interval can lose its input term undetected), and the prose decision rule ('a third of a real pair') is wrong in value and, in the README, in direction (the break-even is kappa=2a/b, about 0.9-1.0). As research it is a correct, honest worked example of a known allocation in M/M/1, missing the data-collection-allocation literature (Freimer & Schruben; Ng & Chick), not a new publishable result.
